name: Screen curfew / dopamine detox

lead: A screen curfew stops phone, computer and TV use some time before bed; a dopamine detox goes further and temporarily abstains from stimulating activities. People in looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities use both to sleep earlier and better, which feeds into skin, less puffiness, energy and focus.

Reference sources describe evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs as able to delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality, which supports the curfew. Dopamine fasting was popularized by psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it targets impulsive behaviors rather than literally lowering dopamine; neuroscientists have criticized the name and the idea of a brain reset. There is no defined protocol or trials for the detox.

paras: People put devices away an hour or more before bed and charge them outside the bedroom. Dopamine detox versions set aside hours or days without social media, games or other high-stimulation activity.
No direct harms are documented for a curfew. Extreme versions of dopamine fasting, such as avoiding food or social contact, have been criticized by clinicians.

web.title: Light effects on circadian rhythm - Wikipedia

angle.text: Cutting screens before bed and taking breaks from stimulation helps you fall asleep earlier and sleep better, which shows in skin, puffiness and energy. The evening-light logic has research behind it; the dopamine framing is disputed by neuroscientists.

lead: A screen curfew means stopping phone, computer and TV use some time before bed, and "dopamine detox" or "dopamine fasting" is a related practice of temporarily abstaining from stimulating activities. In looksmaxxing and self-improvement communities both are discussed as ways to improve sleep and focus.

Reference sources describe evening light from phones, tablets and LEDs as able to delay sleep onset and reduce sleep quality.[1] Dopamine fasting was popularized by psychologist Cameron Sepah, who says it targets impulsive behaviours rather than literally lowering dopamine; neuroscientists have criticized the name and the idea of a brain "reset".[2]

paras: The practice rests on research on evening light, which can delay circadian timing and suppress melatonin, with blue-rich device light cited as most potent.[1] General sleep-hygiene guidance recommends avoiding bright light before bed, although overall evidence that sleep hygiene alone improves insomnia is weak, according to a 2021 meta-analysis cited in reference sources.[3]

Dopamine fasting has no fixed definition: some versions restrict only online technology, others also restrict food, work or conversation.[2] Sepah has said the goal is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not dopamine itself.[2] Critics, including neuroscientist Ciara McCabe, call the idea of resetting the brain scientifically unfounded, and Harvard physician Peter Grinspoon described Sepah's underlying approach as sensible while criticizing extreme versions.[2] Media coverage in 2019 treated it as a Silicon Valley trend.[2]

No studies found of dopamine fasting or a formal screen curfew as defined in these communities. Related research on evening light exposure and sleep exists,[1] and sleep hygiene as a general category has been studied with inconclusive results.[3]

timeline.event: Dopamine fasting receives wide media coverage.[2]
